title: Canadian investigation launched into data breach that exposed millions of IDs
summary: Canada's privacy commissioner has launched an investigation into a data breach at IDScan.net that potentially exposed details from millions of driver's licences and other kinds of government-issued…

image.caption: Canada's privacy commissioner is investigating a data security breach that exposed identification details from driver's licences and other government-issued ID. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada's privacy commissioner has launched an investigation into a data breach at IDScan.net that potentially exposed details from millions of driver's licences and other kinds of government-issued identification from Canada and the U.S.
Privacy commissioner will look into IDScan.net breach involving Canada-issued driver's licences
IDScan.net provides identification verification software to several categories of businesses, from bars and casinos to car rental companies.

Earlier this month, the company published a public notice about a data security incident, stating that "an unauthorized third party may have accessed and/or copied certain customer information stored within their accounts on the IDScan.net cloud."

blocks.text: The company said it was notifying individuals who had potentially been affected and offered free credit monitoring services.

Two days before IDScan.net published its alert, the FBI confirmed it was looking into the reported theft of tens of millions of driver's licences belonging to people in the U.S. and Canada that were being sold on the dark net.
The bureau said it was “looking into the incident” but could not comment “due to the ongoing nature of the investigation.”
The breach could be one of the largest-ever exposures of government-issued identity documents in North America.
Zach Edwards, a threat researcher at the cybersecurity company Infoblox, told Reuters the incident was unprecedented in terms of its sweep.

"There's never been a breach of driver's licences at this scale," said Edwards, who added that he discovered his own license was part of it. Edwards said that the ongoing nature of the breach "means that this attack created legitimate national security risks for high-profile individuals."

Canada's Office of the Privacy Commissioner says it's examining the security safeguards IDScan.net had in place at the time of the breach and whether its actions to notify potentially affected Canadians were adequate.
The probe will also look at whether IDScan.net breached Canada’s federal private-sector privacy laws.
